tldr: By monitoring the latent layers of a VLA model with a lightweight probe, the system accurately predicts both an impending failure and its specific failure mode (such as a grasp failure) before it happens, enabling safe robot recovery behaviors (steering) with statistical guarantees.
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed method, VLA-Tug. (a) VLA backbone embeddings are projected into a latent space via a recurrent encoder (LSTM) to predict a failure score and a failure mode (10 classes). (b) While conventional detectors only react after a failure has already occurred, VLA-Tug captures pre-failure signs to raise an alarm in advance, enabling trajectory correction by an expert model.
overview:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, which unify vision, language, and action, hold great promise as general-purpose embodied intelligence. However, they are extremely brittle under environmental changes (distribution shifts) such as lighting variations or novel textures. The resulting risk of unanticipated failures damaging expensive robots or their surroundings poses a major hurdle to real-world deployment. In response, "steering"—an approach that intervenes in the model's internal activations to correct its trajectory—has attracted attention. Until now, however, there was no reliable trigger to determine "when and how to intervene."

To address this, the authors developed "VLA-Tug," a lightweight and highly accurate runtime monitor. Their key insight was to train on the pre-failure latent representations rather than post-failure data. Instead of showing the model already broken states, training it on patterns leading up to a failure enables early warnings on unseen tasks before it is too late. Furthermore, by employing a statistical hypothesis testing framework (Learn-then-Test), the method provides simultaneous guarantees on both false positive rate (FPR) and early true positive rate (TPR_early), while also classifying failures into 10 distinct failure modes.

Evaluated on a total of 3,180 episodes across simulation (the LIBERO benchmark) and a physical robot (Kinova Gen3), the area under the early failure detection curve on unseen tasks improved by up to 30% over the strongest learned baseline. The authors also demonstrated that statistical bounds remain valid across a high proportion of unseen task runs, and that the probe operates with sub-millisecond latency per step. This paves the way for real-time steering that detects failures proactively to stop or guide the robot safely.
contributions: Achieved early failure detection performance exceeding existing baselines by up to 30% on unseen tasks by focusing training on latent features right before failure onset.

Provided simultaneous statistical guarantees on both false positive rate (FPR) and early true positive rate (TPR_early) using Learn-then-Test, enabling an explicit lower bound on positive predictive value (PPV).
Simultaneously predicted 10 specific failure modes in addition to a simple risk score, enabling informed choices of intervention strategies (such as regrasping or repressing).
Maintained an inference overhead under 1 millisecond (0.12 ms on a GPU), demonstrating real-time failure-avoidance steering on a physical robot.
Released a dataset of 3,180 episodes comprising approximately 289,000 steps extracted from two VLA models, complete with temporal and failure-mode annotations.

sections.heading: Why Do VLAs Need Intervention Triggers Before It Is Too Late?
sections.summary: While VLAs offer impressive dexterity, they remain brittle under distribution shift, where sudden failures can cause severe damage. Making trajectory-correcting steering practical requires a runtime probe that is timely, informative, calibrated, and lightweight.
sections.details:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, which combine internet-scale pre-trained VLMs with robot action experts, are a promising technology capable of handling complex tasks such as screwing bolts or assembling boxes. However, they suffer from a fragility where slight variations in lighting or textures can cause catastrophic behavioral breakdowns, posing the single largest barrier to real-world deployment in factories and homes.

As a countermeasure, "steering"—nudging the model's internal activations to guide it toward desirable behavior—has gained significant attention. It is a powerful technique that can elicit recovery actions that prompting alone cannot unlock. The problem, however, lies in knowing *when* to trigger steering. Prior attempts either applied steering continuously or relied on manually crafted human heuristics, lacking a mechanism for safe, autonomous operation in real environments.

Meanwhile, research on VLA failure detection has progressed, but existing detectors suffer from critical flaws. First, many only constrain the false positive rate (FPR) of misclassifying successes, offering no guarantees on the missed-detection rate (1 - TPR). Second, they are not strictly evaluated on whether alarms are sounded before the actual failure onset, frequently alerting only after it is already too late. Third, outputting only a single scalar risk score leaves the system blind to the underlying cause (e.g., whether it is a missed grasp or an alignment error), preventing the selection of an appropriate recovery action.

The authors argue that a truly practical monitor requires four key properties: (T.) Timely (sensing before failure), (I.) Informative (providing the failure mode), (C.) Calibrated (simultaneously bounding false alarms and missed detections), and (E.) Efficient (running instantly on the edge). To fulfill these requirements, they propose a lightweight probe called "VLA-Tug."

sections.heading: Limitations of Prior Detectors and the Positioning of VLA-Tug
sections.summary: Prior work detected failures using external LLMs, action consistency, or internal representations. However, they left open challenges across three dimensions: temporal anticipation, failure mode identification, and multi-criterion simultaneous calibration.
sections.details:
Several approaches have previously been proposed to detect failures in robot policies.

### Three Lines of Prior Work
- External Evaluators: Methods that monitor policy execution from the outside using world models or external LLM judges.
- Action Consistency: Methods that measure divergence (variance or discrepancies) across generated action chunks or consecutive steps (such as STAC and ActProbe).
- Internal Representation Probing: Methods that score anomalies directly from latent embeddings (backbone activations) inside the policy (such as SAFE).

### Three Limitations of Existing Approaches
However, these prior approaches exhibit distinct shortcomings. The first is the temporal aspect of evaluation and training. Many existing methods evaluate AUROC by labeling entire episodes as failures without considering temporal causality. As a result, they may simply sound an alarm after observing an already damaged state. The second is information granularity. Outputting only a scalar risk value strips away the semantics needed to decide what intervention to take. The third is calibration. While some studies apply Conformal Prediction to control false positive rates, no method has provided simultaneous bounds on both the false positive rate (FPR) and early true positive rate ($\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{early}}$).

### The Uniqueness of VLA-Tug
VLA-Tug resolves these issues all at once. Leveraging the VLA's latent representations, it trains specifically on data prior to failure onset (pre-onset supervision). Furthermore, it introduces the statistical Learn-then-Test framework to simultaneously control FPR and $\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{early}}$, while integrating a 10-class failure mode classification head. This work is the first framework to diagnose the cause at the exact moment of detection and connect directly to immediate steering.

sections.heading: Problem Formulation: Detecting Before Failure and Naming the Cause
sections.summary: The paper mathematically formulates the problem of ensuring the detection time $t_{\mathrm{det}}$ precedes the rollout failure time $t_{\mathrm{fail}}$ while identifying the failure mode $f_{\mathrm{mode}}$. This clarifies the requirements for a monitor that remains reliable even under unseen tasks.
sections.details:
To formalize the task addressed in this work, several key definitions and problem setups are introduced.

### 3.1 Terminology
- Failure Score ($s_t \in \mathbb{R}$): A numeric value at each step $t$ representing the probe's confidence that the trajectory will fail if left unattended.
- Detection Threshold ($h^\star$): The baseline value used to separate failure from success.
- Detection Time ($t_{\mathrm{det}}$): The earliest step at which the failure score exceeds the threshold ($t_{\mathrm{det}} = \min\{t : s_t \geq h^\star\}$). If it never exceeds the threshold, no alarm is raised.
- Failure Time ($t_{\mathrm{fail}}$): The moment the policy commits an irrecoverable error, or when a human operator is forced to intervene (onset).
- Failure Mode ($f_{\mathrm{mode}}$): A high-level failure category from a predefined set of 10 classes, such as grasp failure, placement failure, or lack of progress.

### 3.2 Problem Formulation
A VLA policy $\mathbf{f}_{\text{VLA}}$ takes image observations $\mathbf{o}_t$ and instruction text $\mathbf{p}$, passing through internal embeddings $\mathbf{e}_t$ to output action chunks $\mathbf{a}_{t;0:m-1}$. Each episode carries a success/failure label $Y_i \in \{0, 1\}$; in failure cases ($Y_i=1$), a failure time $t_{\mathrm{fail}}$ and failure mode $f_{\mathrm{mode}}$ are assigned.

The objective is to use a calibration dataset and internal embeddings $\mathbf{e}_t$ to reliably issue an alarm before failure actually occurs ($t_{\mathrm{det}} \leq t_{\mathrm{fail}}$) while predicting the failure mode $f_{\mathrm{mode}}$. Crucially, the statistical guarantees on detection rate and false alarms must hold up practically even on unseen tasks.

sections.heading: How VLA-Tug Works: Latent Probing and Two-Sided Calibration
sections.summary: Backbone embeddings are processed through an LSTM to predict three heads: failure score, failure mode, and CLIP text alignment. By training only on pre-failure states as positive examples, Learn-then-Test simultaneously guarantees FPR and early TPR bounds.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Latent Space Probing and Training Strategy
VLA-Tug is a lightweight neural network that repurposes the rich representations inside a VLA. In this work, the authors target backbone feature representations from $\pi_{0.5}$ (layer 18) and GR00T-N1.7 (layer 16). At each step, token-averaged embeddings from camera views (robot view and wrist view) and the instruction text are concatenated to form a 6,144-dimensional embedding vector $e_t$.

This sequential input is processed by a single-layer LSTM with 256 hidden units. From the resulting latent state $u_t$, the probe branches into three small MLP heads (64 hidden units):
- Failure Score Head: Outputs score $s_t$ via a sigmoid function.
- Failure Mode Head: Outputs a probability distribution $m_t$ over 10 failure mode classes.
- Auxiliary CLIP Head: Aligns the latent representation with the CLIP embedding of a textual description of the current action via contrastive learning.
The entire probe contains only 6.6M parameters (roughly 0.2% of the full model).

The key training innovation is "pre-onset supervision." Conventional failure detectors trained on all steps or post-failure steps of failed trajectories as "failures (label 1)." However, exposing the model to representations after an object has already dropped or the robot has halted only teaches it what a broken state looks like, not the precursor signs of impending failure. VLA-Tug therefore labels only the steps prior to failure onset $t_{\mathrm{fail}}$ as positive examples of impending failure, completely excluding steps from $t_{\mathrm{fail}}$ onward from the loss computation. Successful episodes treat all steps as negative examples (label 0).

### 4.2 Uncertainty Quantification and Statistical Guarantees
For safe robotic operation, the authors adopt the Learn-then-Test (LTT) framework. Users specify a maximum tolerable false positive rate $\alpha$ and a minimum desired early true positive rate $\beta$:
$$\mathbb{P}\left(\mathrm{FPR}(h^\star) \leq \alpha \quad \text{and} \quad \mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{early}}(h^\star) \geq \beta\right) \geq 1 - \delta$$
Testing candidate thresholds on a calibration set yields a threshold $h^\star$ that satisfies both criteria with probability at least $1-\delta$ (90% in this work). If no candidate threshold satisfies the conditions, the system refrains from reckless compromises and raises an "Abstain" flag.

To provide practitioners with an intuitive metric, Bayes' rule is also used to derive a lower bound on the positive predictive value (PPV)—the probability that an alarm indicates an actual failure. Computing this bound is uniquely possible because VLA-Tug simultaneously guarantees early TPR.

sections.heading: A Large-Scale Failure Dataset: 3,180 Episodes with Temporal Annotations
sections.summary: Across simulated environments (LIBERO family) and a physical robot, the authors built a dataset of roughly 289,000 steps spanning 3,180 episodes. A high-precision VLM annotation pipeline was used to assign detailed labels for failure onsets and failure modes.
sections.details:
### Benchmarks and Data Splits for Generalization
To evaluate VLA-Tug, the authors utilized the simulated LIBERO benchmark, LIBERO-Occ with camera occlusions, LIBERO-X covering diverse tasks, and 8 real-world tasks on a Kinova Gen3 robot. The VLA policies tested were $\pi_{0.5}$ and GR00T-N1.7.

To rigorously assess generalization to unseen environments (robustness to distribution shift), LIBERO-X was divided into three splits based on shift severity:
- new-task: Individual tasks are held out for testing (combinations of skills and objects are familiar, making the shift mild).
- new-signature: Entire combinations of "skill, object, and spatial relation" are held out (individual components are seen, but the composition is novel).
- new-skill: Specific skills (such as pressing a button) are held out entirely from training (the most severe distribution shift).

### An Efficient Automated Annotation Pipeline
To label these vast episodes, the authors built a three-stage pipeline leveraging Gemini (gemini-3.5-flash). After coarsely identifying failure times and failure modes across full videos, slow-motion footage around the failure point determines the precise frame-level failure onset $t_{\mathrm{fail}}$. Segment-level action descriptions (timelines) were also generated every 3 seconds. Failure modes were categorized into 10 classes, such as "wrong_object," "grasp_failure," "press_failure," and "stuck_or_no_progress."

This pipeline yielded a highly accurate annotated dataset at an extremely low cost of roughly 1 cent per failed episode. All 3,180 episodes and over 288,000 backbone embedding vectors have been open-sourced.

captions.F3: Dataset annotation example. For videos of a successful episode (top) and a failed episode (bottom), 3-second timeline descriptions, a precise frame-level failure onset (10.3 s), and one of 10 failure modes (grasp failure) are annotated.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Early Detection, Statistical Bounds, Mode Prediction, and Real-Robot Steering
sections.summary: VLA-Tug outperformed existing baselines by up to 30% in early detection on unseen tasks while exhibiting remarkable robustness in maintaining statistical bounds. With an inference latency of just 0.12 ms, it also successfully demonstrated failure-avoidance steering on a physical robot.
sections.details:
The authors conducted comprehensive experiments structured around five questions (Q1 to Q5).

### 6.1 Early Detection Performance (Q1. Timeliness)
Performance was compared using the area under the curve ($\mathrm{AUROC}_{\mathrm{early}}$) between the fraction of failures detected before failure onset ($\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{early}}$) and the false positive rate (FPR $\in [0, 0.4]$). Baselines spanned distance-based metrics (Mahalanobis, k-NN), action-consistency metrics (STAC, ActProbe, FailureSpot), and latent-probing metrics (SAFE).
VLA-Tug achieved top performance across nearly all unseen task conditions. Compared to the strongest learned baseline, SAFE-LSTM, VLA-Tug was comparable on new-task (-1%), but pulled ahead as the distribution shift intensified: +14% on new-signature and +30% on the most challenging new-skill split. Supervising on pre-failure precursors rather than post-failure states proved crucial for generalizing to unseen tasks.

### 6.2 Calibration Verification (Q2. Calibration)
The validity of Learn-then-Test bounds was evaluated. On the in-distribution test set, target FPR and $\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{early}}$ bounds were satisfied across 100% of certified runs. Even under severe unseen task shifts, FPR bounds were preserved in 40% to 86% of runs. In contrast, existing methods (such as Max-Conformal) maintained bounds in at most 21% of unseen task runs, leading to severe safety breaches. Furthermore, when guarantees cannot be met, LTT refrains from guessing and abstains, preventing hazardous executions.

### 6.3 Failure Mode Prediction and Efficiency (Q3. & Q4.)
When predicting 10 failure modes from latent representations on unseen LIBERO-X tasks, Top-1 accuracy improved by up to 79% over a majority-class baseline, with strong gains on real-world tasks as well. Top-3 accuracy provided sufficient information to guide appropriate recovery strategies.
Inference time on an RTX 4090 was a mere 0.12 ms (0.9 ms on a CPU). This represents just 0.2% of the VLA backbone computation time (approximately 54 ms), introducing negligible overhead into a 400 ms control loop.

### 6.4 Steering Demonstrations in Simulation and on Real Robots (Q5. Steering)
The authors conducted closed-loop experiments where probe alarms and predicted failure modes triggered automated robot corrections. In simulation, when a policy was about to place a bowl into the wrong basket, an early alarm paused the policy, guided the end-effector to the correct left basket, and resumed execution to complete the task. On the physical Kinova arm performing a "place mushroom on plate" task, detecting an impending grasp failure allowed the system to nudge the camera view, avoid a table collision, and guide the rollout to success.

captions.F5: Early failure detection curves (early true positive rate TPR_early vs. FPR) on in-distribution tasks (top row) and unseen tasks (bottom row). VLA-Tug (green line) shows superior detection accuracy that widens the gap over baselines, particularly under severe distribution shifts such as unseen skills (new-skill, rightmost).
captions.F6: Demonstration of failure-avoidance steering in simulation (left) and on a physical robot (right). The moment the probe's failure score crosses the threshold, the policy is paused, and a correction (guiding the end-effector or camera) based on the predicted failure mode turns an otherwise failing trajectory into a success.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook: Towards Safe Autonomous Robots
sections.summary: The authors introduced VLA-Tug, a runtime probe that combines timeliness, informativeness, statistical guarantees, and high efficiency. By targeting representations immediately preceding failure, it drastically improves robustness to distribution shift and lays the foundation for safe VLA steering.
sections.details:
This paper presented VLA-Tug, a runtime monitor designed for the safe deployment of VLA models in the physical world. By probing VLA latent layers and training specifically on pre-failure behaviors, the monitor issues warnings on unseen tasks before it is too late. Providing dual statistical guarantees that simultaneously bound false alarms and missed detections, while also identifying the failure mode, represents a significant advantage over conventional failure detectors.

### Limitations Acknowledged in the Paper
- Calibration Assumptions: The statistical guarantees depend on exchangeability between calibration and test distributions; under extreme distribution shifts, theoretical bounds gradually degrade (though empirical degradation remains graceful).
- Latent Layer Selection: The study probed specific layers (such as layer 16 in GR00T), leaving an exhaustive comparison of which backbone layers hold the most generalizable failure signals to future work.
- Steering Design: Interventions implemented in this study relied on simple heuristics; optimizing and systematically benchmarking the intervention algorithms themselves was beyond the scope of this paper.

### Future Work
Looking ahead, the authors plan to investigate online updating of probes and calibration bounds during deployment, as well as an agentic architecture where lightweight VLA-Tug edge alarms trigger large cloud-based VLMs/LLMs to plan and execute recovery strategies.

sections.heading: Appendix: Latent Space Visualizations and Full Baseline Comparisons
sections.summary: PCA visualizations of the probe's latent space demonstrate clear separation between success and failure trajectories as well as distinct failure modes. The appendix also compiles comprehensive performance curves across all baseline methods and experimental splits.
sections.details:
### Latent Space Visualizations (E.1 & E.2)
To investigate what VLA-Tug learns, the authors visualized raw backbone embeddings, LSTM latent states, and MLP hidden outputs using Principal Component Analysis (PCA). In the raw VLA backbone space, successful steps and pre-failure steps overlap heavily, making discrimination difficult. After passing through VLA-Tug's LSTM, however, the two form cleanly separated clusters. Furthermore, in the failure mode head's layer, distinct error causes—such as grasp failures versus placement failures—map cleanly onto separate regions.

### Early Detection Curves Across All Settings (C.3)
Comprehensive early true positive rate ($\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{early}}$) versus false positive rate (FPR) curves are detailed across six experimental splits: LIBERO-10 ($\pi_{0.5}$ and GR00T), LIBERO-X (new-task, new-signature, new-skill), and the physical Kinova robot. Action-consistency metrics like STAC and ActProbe were poorly suited for early detection, as their scores spike only after physical execution visibly degrades. In contrast, VLA-Tug directly monitors latent layers, picking up subtle internal perturbations before errors manifest physically and consistently delivering superior early detection.

captions.F7: Full view of early detection performance curves across all six evaluated settings (various LIBERO benchmarks and physical robot) for in-distribution tasks (top row) and unseen tasks (bottom row). VLA-Tug (solid green line) consistently achieves superior detection rates across a wide range of FPR thresholds.

takeaways: Training failure detectors on pre-onset data rather than post-failure data is essential, serving as the primary driver for generalizing to unseen tasks.
Bounding early true positive rate (TPR_early) alongside false positive rate (FPR) enables practitioners to compute meaningful lower bounds on positive predictive value (PPV).
Predicting the underlying failure mode concurrently with an anomaly score provides actionable context that directly enables automated robot recovery (steering).
Probing VLA backbone latent representations is extraordinarily lightweight (~0.1 ms), allowing seamless real-time integration without bottlenecking robot control loops.
limitations: Statistical calibration bounds rely on distributional similarity between calibration and test data, meaning theoretical guarantees degrade under extreme distribution shifts.
The choice of which internal VLA backbone layers to probe relies on empirical heuristics, lacking an exhaustive search for the optimal layer.
Steering interventions following failure detection remain restricted to simple heuristics, leaving the establishment of general-purpose recovery algorithms for future work.
